profile.name: Sumazau
profile.insight: Dancers mimic the graceful flight of an eagle, their arms flapping in rhythm to the deep, resonant beat of hanging gongs that have echoed across Sabah’s paddy fields for generations.
profile.profile: The Sumazau is a traditional dance of the Kadazan-Dusun and Murut peoples of Sabah, Malaysia, performed during the Kaamatan harvest festival and other significant social or ritual occasions. Dancers move in pairs, shifting weight and flapping their arms to imitate the flight of an eagle. The performance is accompanied by a specific ensemble of hanging gongs and drums, known as the sompogogungan and gandang. It remains a vital expression of cultural identity, recognized as a national heritage in Malaysia.
profile.profile_long: The Sumazau is a traditional dance performed by the Kadazan people from the Penampang and Papar districts, as well as the Dusun and Murut communities of Sabah, Malaysia. It is deeply embedded in the cultural life of these groups, serving both ceremonial and celebratory functions. Historically, the dance has been performed during traditional rituals such as the magang after headhunting, for spirits inhabiting a bangkavan, and during the moginum ceremony. In contemporary times, it is most widely recognized for its role in the Kaamatan harvest festival, where it honors the traditional rice spirit, as well as at weddings and major social gatherings. The dance is performed by male and female pairs dressed in traditional attire, often featuring the sinombiaka—a black cloth ensemble accented with gold braid. Women accessorize with the tangkong (brass rings) and the himpogot (a belt of British trade dollar coins), while men wear the sigar, a colorful headcloth. The movement is characterized by a rhythmic, bird-like imitation, specifically that of an eagle, which dancers would have observed from the paddy fields. The dance begins with dancers shifting their weight from foot to foot while keeping their knees bent and arms swinging at their sides. Upon a cue from a male dancer, the group transitions to a position where arms are outstretched and feet are on tiptoes. Men perform a gentle rolling motion with their arms, while women keep their elbows bent downwards and raise their heels slightly. This movement is set to the music of the sompogogungan, a set of six to seven hanging gongs, and the gandang, a double-headed drum. The music is defined by a repetitive, interlocking rhythmic pattern that continues until the dance sequence concludes. The dance is not merely a performance but a recognized national heritage, protected and celebrated by both the Malaysian federal and Sabah state governments. Its significance has persisted into the 21st century, where it has been adapted for religious modesty standards and featured in high-profile events, including royal visits and international performances at Westminster Abbey. The dance remains a living tradition, practiced by communities across Sabah and serving as a symbol of self-expression and cultural identity.

sections.origins_and_history: The Sumazau originates from the Kadazan-Dusun and Murut peoples of Sabah, Malaysia, with deep roots in agricultural and ritual life.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers move in pairs, shifting weight with bent knees and swinging arms. A male dancer cues a transition to an outstretched arm position on tiptoes, mimicking an eagle.
sections.music_and_instruments: The ensemble consists of the sompogogungan (six to seven hanging gongs), the gandang (a double-headed drum), and sometimes a kulintangan (gong-chime or metallophone).
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear the sinombiaka (black cloth with gold braid). Women wear tangkong (brass rings) and himpogot (coin belts); men wear the sigar (headcloth).
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed for the Kaamatan harvest festival, weddings, and rituals like the magang (post-headhunting) and moginum.
sections.notable_figures: Norbert Andilah (viral PPE dancer), Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah (Queen consort of Malaysia).
sections.regional_variants: Magarang (Liwan Dusun), Sumayau (Lotud Dusun), Mongigol (Tindal Dusun), Mongigol Sumundai (Rungus), Mangalai (Tinagas Dusun).
sections.lineage: Indigenous Sabah traditions of the Kadazan-Dusun and Murut peoples.

profile.sacred_note: The dance is performed in ritual contexts such as the Monogit healing ceremony and post-headhunting rites; outsiders should respect the cultural significance and ritual nature of these events.

basic_steps: Shift weight from foot to foot with knees bent.
Swing arms at sides in time to the music.
Extend arms outward with rolling or downward-bent elbow motion.
teaching.rhythm: Interlocking rhythmic pattern of gongs and drums.
teaching.level_notes: Beginner-friendly, focus on rhythmic weight shifting and arm posture.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Interlocking parts starting with the gandang, followed by the sompogogungan.
music_profile.sound_description: A steady, interlocking percussive sound dominated by the deep resonance of hanging gongs and the rhythmic beat of a double-headed drum.

movement_profile.footwork: Weight shifting from foot to foot, transitioning to tiptoes.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Arms flapping at sides or outstretched with rolling motion/bent elbows.
movement_profile.partnering: Male dancer cues the group for position changes.

signature_moves.name: Eagle Flight
signature_moves.description: Arms outstretched and flapping to imitate the departure of an eagle.

drills: Swing arms in time to a steady beat.

claims.text: The movement imitates the departure of an eagle, which would have been visible from paddy fields.
claims.quote: This move imitates the departure of a bird, specifically an eagle, which would have been visible from paddy fields.

claims.text: The dance is accompanied by a sompogogungan, a set of six to seven hanging gongs, and a gandang drum.

claims.quote: It is also performed during Kaamatan in honour of the traditional rice spirit, besides wedding celebrations, the 40th night of a deceased person's passing and other major social gatherings.
